hero.subtitle: I'm a CTO of 15 years and an engineer of 20. I come in for weeks, not quarters — to tell you what's real about your engineering, fix what's breaking, and leave you with a plan your board can read. Working US Eastern hours.

about.title: Who I Work With
paragraphs: You're a PE operating partner. The deal closed and the technical reality showed up — fragile delivery, key-person risk, an undocumented codebase, security gaps nobody surfaced before signing. You need someone who can tell you how bad it is in two weeks, not two quarters, and who has run engineering organisations rather than only audited them.
You're a founder raising in the next six to twelve months. Your investors will run technical due diligence on you. You would rather find out what they'll find before they find it.

You have engineers but nobody owns the technology. Five to fifteen people shipping, decisions made by whoever argues longest, and a roadmap that's really a backlog. You don't need a full-time CTO at $400–600k all-in. You need one for a day or two a week.

work.title: How an Engagement Runs
paragraphs: Every engagement starts with a fixed-scope, fixed-price diagnostic — a two-week due diligence sprint or a 30-day technical assessment. You get a written deliverable before you commit to anything longer.

Days 1–3: orientation and artifact review — architecture, repositories, CI/CD, incident history, dependency and licence map, cloud spend. Days 4–7: interviews and walkthroughs with the engineers, not only the CTO. Days 8–10: synthesis, pressure-tested against your actual underwriting questions.

You receive a risk register with severity and confidence levels, initiative cards with cost and sequencing, an explicit statement of what I could not access and what that leaves unknown, and a 60-minute readout with your team.
If it makes sense afterwards, the diagnostic converts into a fractional CTO retainer at one to three days a week. If it doesn't, you still own the assessment — and I'll tell you who to call instead.

achievements.title: Track Record
achievements.subtitle: Twenty years building software. Fifteen as CTO. Numbers, not adjectives.

mentorist.title: Mentorist
mentorist.shortDescription: Consumer subscription product I founded, funded and scaled — then rebuilt end to end on my own.
mentorist.revenue: 6-figure ARR · €550k raised · passed investor technical DD
mentorist.fullStory:
Mentorist is a consumer subscription product that helps people implement what they read rather than only summarising it. It reached six-figure annual revenue and raised €550k.

I ran it as founder and CTO: architecture, delivery, hiring, vendor decisions and investor relations — including the technical due diligence that came with the raise. That's the same process I now run from the other side of the table, which is a large part of why I'm useful at it.

The current version I rebuilt end to end on my own — frontend, backend, UX, infrastructure and content — using AI tooling throughout.

iqelite.title: IQElite
iqelite.shortDescription: Psychometric matching platform. I took over as CEO with the company losing money and turned it profitable in 90 days.
iqelite.revenue: 8M registered users · break-even in 90 days · profitable for 8 years
iqelite.fullStory:
I joined IQElite in Barcelona as co-founder and CTO, running technology. After eighteen months I took over as CEO.

The company had a five-person team and was losing money. Within three months of me taking over we reached break-even, and stayed profitable for the next eight years.

The platform reached 8 million registered users on psychometric matching — IQ, personality, EQ and compatibility testing. It declined later as Tinder and Bumble reshaped the category.

This is the engagement I draw on most. A small team, a broken P&L, and no time — which is what most post-acquisition technical situations actually look like.

neurony.title: Neurony Szaleją
neurony.shortDescription: Consumer brand where I owned acquisition end to end — creative strategy, media buying and the landing pages underneath it.
neurony.revenue: 6-figure yearly revenue · scaled on paid acquisition
neurony.fullStory:
Neurony Szaleją sells products for mothers of small children. In 2024 the business ran almost entirely on organic reach and had no repeatable acquisition engine.

I owned the whole stack of that problem: creative strategy, Meta campaign structure, and then custom React landing pages when the conversion rate turned out to be the real constraint rather than the traffic. We ran the tests in sequence and fixed the funnel step by step.

The brand reached six-figure annual revenue and is expanding into other markets. I include it here because it's the clearest example of the thing I actually do: the acquisition problem and the engineering problem were the same problem, and one person solving both was faster than two people negotiating about it.

hackyeah.title: 1st Place — HackYeah 2025
hackyeah.shortDescription: Built and shipped a working product in 24 hours with AI tooling, with a team formed on the day. Won.
hackyeah.fullStory:
I went to HackYeah 2025 in Kraków without a team, met two people on site, and we entered the live-run category as a three-person group.

We built a retirement simulation game in 24 hours and took first place. I leaned on AI tooling heavily to carry the workload — roughly 14,000 lines of code over the run.

It's a small thing, but it's recent, it's verifiable, and it's the honest answer to whether a twenty-year engineer can actually work at AI-native speed rather than just talk about it.

expertise.title: What I'm Hired For
expertise.subtitle: Four angles on one question: whether the technology works, and whether the business it supports does. Usually those are two different consultants and two different invoices.

performanceMarketing.title: Technical Due Diligence
performanceMarketing.shortDescription: Two-week sprints for investors and founders: what's actually true about the technology, tied to your underwriting questions.

details.intro: I run technical diligence for investors, and for founders who want to see what their investors will see. Two weeks, fixed price, written deliverable — answered against your specific questions rather than a generic checklist.
whatYouGetItems: A risk register with severity, likelihood and my confidence level on each item
Initiative cards — what fixing it costs, how long it takes, and in what order
An explicit statement of what I could not access, and what that leaves unknown
A 60-minute readout with your deal team, plus follow-up questions answered for 30 days
details.closing: I don't write "review security". I answer "is privileged access controlled, and what does it cost to fix if it isn't". Two weeks. $15,000. Fixed.

fullStack.title: Fractional CTO
fullStack.shortDescription: One to three days a week, with decision rights — not advice from the sidelines.

details.intro: For companies with engineers and nobody owning engineering. I take the decisions that are currently being made by whoever argues longest, and I take responsibility for them.
details.typicalStackFrontend: A technical roadmap tied to a funding or revenue milestone, not a wish list
details.typicalStackBackend: Engineering hiring — role specs, technical screens, architecture interviews
details.typicalStackInfrastructure: Security and delivery baseline — access control, backups, CI/CD, incident runbooks
details.whatThisMeansBody: You get someone with the authority to say no — to a feature, a hire or a vendor — and the standing to make it stick. That's the part advisory can't do. Engagements start after a diagnostic, run a minimum of three months, and include a written hand-off plan to a permanent CTO from day one.
details.closing: A full-time CTO costs $400–600k all-in in the first year once you count base, benefits and recruiting. This is the same judgement at a fraction of it. Retainers start at $10,000 per month.

productUx.title: Unit Economics
productUx.shortDescription: €700k+ of ad budget deployed, much of it my own. I can tell you whether the business the code supports actually works.

details.intro: Most people who assess technology have never carried a number. I've deployed over €700,000 in Meta ad spend — much of it my own money — building and scaling consumer subscription products.
approachItems: CAC and payback period against the real retention curve, not the one in the deck
Whether the acquisition channel is durable or is renting growth from a platform
Where the funnel leaks — and whether that's a product problem or a marketing one
Whether the tracking and attribution can be trusted before anyone acts on them
examplesItems: €700k+ deployed across Meta, a large share of it at my own risk
Consumer subscription products taken from zero to six-figure ARR
A consumer brand scaled to six-figure annual revenue on paid acquisition
details.closing: When I tell you a company's unit economics don't survive contact with reality, I'm not reading it off a spreadsheet. I've been on the wrong side of that number with my own capital.

aiTools.title: AI in Production
aiTools.shortDescription: Most AI pilots never ship. I assess the ones that should, and say plainly when one shouldn't.

details.intro: Enterprises spent tens of billions on generative AI last year and most executives report no measurable financial return. The gap is almost never the model. It's evaluation, reliability, and the absence of anyone willing to say a pilot has failed.
proofItems: Rebuilt an entire production consumer app solo, with AI tooling throughout
~14,000 lines shipped in 24 hours at HackYeah 2025 — first place
Twenty years shipping software, so I know what production actually costs to run
details.howItHelpsBody: Assess whether an AI initiative is a real capability or a demo with a roadmap attached. Build the evaluation harness that tells you when it regresses. And say plainly when the honest answer is that it should be bought rather than built.
details.idealUseBody: Investors underwriting an AI claim in a target company, and operators who have already spent once and want the second attempt to actually reach production.

cta.title: Not sure whether the problem is the technology or the business?
cta.subtitle: That's usually the question, and it's usually answered by two different consultants who don't talk to each other. Two weeks, fixed price, and a written answer you can hand to your board — whether or not we work together afterwards.
